fetched_contents.text: Design and Optimization of Piezoelectric Cantilever Beam Vibration Energy Harvester Abstract Piezoelectric cantilever beams are commonly utilized to harvest energy from environmental vibrations due to their simple structures. This paper optimizes a single crystal trapezoidal hollow structure piezoelectric cantilever beam vibration energy harvester with a copper substrate to achieve high energy density at a low frequency. Finite element analysis (FEA) is adopted to optimize the size of the copper substrate at first, and the piezoelectric energy harvester (PEH) is further optimized with a trapezoidal hollow structure under the optimal size of the copper substrate. The developed PEH with a trapezoidal hollow structure (La = 20 mm, Lb = 15 mm, and Lh = 40 mm), with a copper substrate of 80 mm × 33 mm × 0.2 mm, can obtain the best output performance. Under the condition of 1 g acceleration, the resonance frequency and peak voltage output were 23.29 Hz and 40.4 V, respectively. Compared with the unhollowed PEH, the developed trapezoidal hollow structure PEH can reduce its resonant frequency by 12.18% and increase output voltage by 34.67%, while also supplying a power density of 7.24 mW/cm3. This study verified the feasibility of the optimized design through simulation and experimental comparison. Keywords: optimization, FEA, PEH, hollow structure, high energy density 1. Introduction Despite the fact that many electronic devices still rely solely on chemical batteries for power in the face of the miniaturization trend of embedded electronic devices and sensors [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8], traditional batteries, due to their massive size [5,6,9] and their need for timely replacement or recharging [6,7,8,10,11,12], no longer meet the power needs of some electronic devices [8,13,14,15]. With the development of electronic integration technology and microelectromechanical technology, the power consumption of some commonly used sensing and transmitting modules can be reduced to hundreds of nW, which makes it possible to use energy harvesting technology to power low power electronic devices [16]. Harvesting energy from the environment to power electronic devices or charge batteries has the potential to improve this situation. As reported, solar, wind, geothermal, water, and vibration energies can all be harvested from our environment [8,17,18,19,20]. Vibrations can be found all around us, such as the vibration of a car passing by, a machine in operation, or a tree branch in the wind. Vibration energy harvesting can, thus, be applied in a variety of environments [7,8,13,21,22]. Diverse transduction mechanisms based on piezoelectric, electromagnetic, and electrostatic generation principles have been utilized to convert vibration into electrical energy [13,14,23,24,25,26,27,28,29]. Due to their higher energy density and simpler structure [4,19], piezoelectric energy harvesters (PEHs) have attracted attention [5,6,7,10,12,15]. In addition, piezoelectric materials are well suited for flexible and stretchable devices, and can be easily scaled in micro and nano devices [4,8,12,30]. When vibrations from the external environment drive the deformation of the piezoelectric material, opposite charges are generated on two opposite surfaces of the piezoelectric material due to the piezoelectric effect [31]. A voltage difference is created between the two opposing surfaces, causing the charges in the circuit to travel in a specific direction. A current can be detected in the circuit. Piezoelectric energy harvesters with cantilever beam structures are widely applied because of their simple structure and significant deformation under vibration [5,12]. In order to improve the output performance of the piezoelectric cantilever, researchers have made many improvements to the cantilever. Karadag, C.V. et al. [32] optimizes the shape of the cantilever beam and adopts a curved beam. In the two cases of the beam with no tip mass and a 5 g tip mass, compared with the regular triangular beam, the optimized beam shows a 22% and 29% increase in strain uniformity, respectively. Wu, H. et al. [33] designed a two-degrees-of-freedom piezoelectric cantilever beam, comprising of one main cantilever beam and an inner secondary cantilever beam. By adjusting the masses, the first two resonant frequencies can be tuned very close, resulting in a wider effective operating bandwidth. Xiong, Y. et al. [34] designed a cantilever beam with a rectangular hollow middle layer, which reduced the resonance frequency of the cantilever beam and increased the output voltage. Wang, L. et al. [35] designed a hollow triangular piezoelectric cantilever beam suitable for the random low frequency vibration environment of transportation infrastructure. Wang, B. et al. [36] designed a piezoelectric cantilever beam with a trapezoidal hole, and this piezoelectric cantilever beam obtained a power density of 8.932 mW/cm3 at an acceleration of 1.5 g. The triangular hole, rectangular hole, and trapezoidal hole were compared in Wang B’s research, and the PEH with a trapezoidal hole was proved to have the best performance. However, for PEH with a trapezoidal hole, the influence of the direction and area of the trapezoid on the output have yet to be investigated in detail. However, piezoelectric energy harvesting technology still faces some challenges. Harvesters with low frequency, high power density, and good stability are urgently needed to meet the requirements of energy development [15,37]. In recent years, the main contradiction is that the vibration source requires the device to match a lower resonance frequency. In addition, material optimization, substrate replacement, and geometry change are the main methods currently utilized for the optimization of harvesters [38,39]. fetched_contents.text: Harnessing vibrations: A review on structural architecture and design ideology of the cantilever beam based piezoelectric energy harvesters Introduction In recent decades, the exponential growth in IoT has led to an increase in the deployment of small-scale electronic devices in diverse environments, from industrial applications to medical and environmental monitoring systems [1,2]. These devices are often powered by batteries, which require periodic replacement, posing significant challenges, particularly in remote or hard-to-access locations [3]. The limitations of battery power in terms of life span, maintenance, and environmental impact have led researchers to explore alternative methods of powering such devices. Moreover, their disposal into the environment causes harmful effects. Today, as awareness of their harmful effects and the need to reduce our reliance on them as mobile energy sources increases, it is essential to find alternative solutions [4]. One promising solution is the concept of energy harvesting, which aims to capture and convert ambient energy from the surrounding environment into usable electrical power. In addition to providing clean energy, unlike batteries, this enables an extended lifespan for electronic devices by supplying unlimited power [5]. Among the various forms, vibration energy stands out as one of the most commonly available forms of ambient energy in the environment [4]. Fig. 1 presents the estimated operating frequency ranges of various mechanical energy sources, based on findings from several research studies [4,[6], [7], [8]]. Hence, this has significant potential, especially for low-power applications such as wireless sensor networks (WSNs), microelectromechanical systems (MEMS), and other embedded devices [9,10]. Harvesting energy from vibrations is a well-established concept, and multiple mechanisms have been proposed to capture this form of energy. These mechanisms primarily include electromagnetic, electrostatic, and piezoelectric methods [11]. Electrostatic energy harvesting, though flexible with high conversion rates, needs an external power source to start up [12], while electromagnetic systems are efficient but bulky and complex, which makes them less suitable for MEMS applications [13,14]. In contrast, piezoelectric energy harvesting has emerged as one of the most promising technologies due to its simplicity, high energy density, and ability to operate efficiently in various environments [15]. Additionally, the average energy density of piezoelectric converters is three times higher, making them a prominent choice for mechanical-to-electrical energy conversion [16]. In many cases, the mechanical energy from sources such as acoustics [17], water flow [18], wind [19], human movement [19], and infrastructure vibrations like railway tracks [20] is first converted into vibrations, which are then transformed into electricity through piezoelectric materials. In 1880, the Curie brothers made a significant discovery with quartz (SiO₂) crystals and identified the direct piezoelectric effect [21]. This effect refers to the ability of certain materials to convert mechanical stress into an electrical signal, such as polarization, electric displacement, or an electric field. Later, they also demonstrated that the process could work in the opposite direction, where an applied electric field causes a mechanical response in specific crystals, which is known as indirect piezoelectricity. These direct and indirect effects enable the material to serve as both actuators and power generators [22]. There are mainly three types of material that can produce these effects, these are piezoelectric single crystals, piezoelectric polymers, and piezoelectric ceramics [21]. Piezoelectric single crystals like quartz and lithium niobate were essential in early sensor development but are brittle and difficult to process. On the contrary, polymers like polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) offer flexibility and biocompatibility but suffer from weak piezoelectricity. However, piezoelectric ceramics such as lead zirconate titanate, lead titanate, and barium titanate overcome these limitations by providing high electromechanical conversion efficiency and better temperature stability [23]. Piezoelectric materials consist of dipole molecules, and when stress is exerted on them, their molecular structure undergoes a transformation, leading to a separation of charges. The dipole molecules align with positive charges accumulating on one side and negative charges on the other, resulting in the generation of a voltage [24]. The coupled electromechanical behavior of piezoelectric materials can be described using two linearized constitutive equations. Direct piezoelectric effect:Di=eijσEj+dimdσm Indirect piezoelectric effect:εk=djkiEj+SkmEσm In these equations, Di represents the dielectric displacement, measured in either N/mV or C/m2, while εk is the strain vector. The electric field vector, denoted by Ej, is measured in V/m, and σm is the stress vector, expressed in N/m2. The piezoelectric constants include the coefficients dimd and djkc, measured in m/V or C/N, the dielectric permittivity eijσ, in either N/V2 or F/M, and SkmE, which represents the elastic compliance matrix, measured in m2/N. The superscripts d and i refer to the direct and indirect effects, while the superscripts σ and E indicate that the values are taken under constant stress and constant electric field conditions, respectively. Two piezoelectric modes, d31 and d33, are widely employed in piezoelectric microdevices. These modes are differentiated by the arrangement of the electric field in relation to the strain. In the d31 mode, the electric field is oriented perpendicularly to the direction of the applied strain, whereas in the d33 mode, the electric field aligns parallel to the strain. fetched_contents.text: Optimal design of unimorph-type cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvesters using level set-based topology optimization by considering manufacturability 1. Introduction Piezoelectric energy harvesters convert mechanical energy into electrical energy through the piezoelectric effect. These devices have gained significant attention in recent years owing to their potential to scavenge energy from various sources such as vibrations [1], [2] and fluid flow [3]. The design of a piezoelectric energy harvester plays a critical role in determining its efficiency and performance [4]. Various piezoelectric energy harvester designs, including cantilever beams, multilayered structures, and cylindrical structures, have been proposed and studied [5], [6]. The unimorph cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester has several advantages over other piezoelectric energy harvester designs. A unimorph cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester consists of a cantilever beam with one end fixed and the other end free to move. The beam is typically composed of two primary domains: a substrate domain and a piezoelectric material domain. Additionally, it includes electrode domains for electrical energy extraction. When the device is subjected to external vibrations or mechanical loads, the beam bends, causing mechanical strain in the piezoelectric domain. This strain generates electrical energy through the piezoelectric effect. The simple and compact design of this harvester makes it suitable for applications where size and weight are critical factors, such as in portable or wearable devices. Furthermore, the unimorph cantilevered design allows easy integration with other systems, such as sensors or wireless transmitters [7]. However, the performance of a unimorph cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester is limited by the amount of mechanical energy harvested from external vibrations. To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored the use of advanced materials and optimization techniques to improve their performance. Some studies have investigated piezoelectric materials with improved electromechanical coupling factors to enhance the piezoelectric effect and improve the efficiency of energy conversion [8], [9]. Other researchers have focused on designing the geometry of the cantilever beam and piezoelectric element for maximum energy output. For instance, rectangular, triangular, and trapezoidal shapes have been proposed for unimorph piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters [10]. However, as these structures have simple geometries, significant improvements can be achieved using topological optimization techniques [11]. Among the early forays in the topology optimization of piezoelectric materials, the study by Silva et al. [12] stood out as a pioneering study. This study explored the optimal design of periodic piezocomposites and underscored the profound impact of the unit cell topology on the performance of piezoelectric materials. Their insights provided a foundational framework for subsequent advancements in the field. The optimization of a piezoelectric energy harvester requires meticulous attention to numerous parameters, including the geometry and material properties of the piezoelectric element, the resonant frequency of the device, and the electrical load impedance. Zheng et al. [13] introduced a topology optimization technique to maximize the harvesting performance of piezoelectric energy harvesters. Rupp et al. [14] conceived a design for a piezoelectric energy harvester integrated with an external electrical circuit with due regard to the electrical load impedance. Kögl and Silva [15] advanced the “PEAMAP-P” analysis model, specifically tailored for the analytical modeling of piezoelectric materials. Their design paradigm singularly targeted the piezoelectric material domain and deliberately omitted the substrate domain. Kang and Tong [16] considered both the piezoelectric material and electrode domains in their design. Adding a unique perspective, Zhang and Kang [17] focused on the dynamic responses in piezoelectric structures, emphasizing transient load optimization. Their approach highlights the need for a precisely tailored design in active-control smart structures. Chen et al. [18] and Luo et al. [19] designed tubular energy harvesting devices made of multiple materials. Notably, they employed level set-based topology optimization to eliminate grayscale discrepancies between the material and void domains. He et al. [20] and de Almeida et al. [21] focused on designing the thickness profile of a piezoelectric energy harvester by considering the piezoelectric material, substrate, and electrode domains. In addition, Kim and Lee [22] optimized both the substrate and piezoelectric material domains. They delineated distinct objective functions for each domain and sequentially optimized the substrate and piezoelectric film structures. Similarly, in the field of acoustic energy focusing, Yoon et al. [23] demonstrated the application of topology optimization for piezoelectric acoustic focusers. By considering the intricate interactions between the electric, mechanical, and acoustic phenomena, their approach offers a more comprehensive understanding and optimization of piezoelectric devices in acoustically challenging environments. In a notable advancement, Salas et al. [24] extended topology optimization of piezoelectric actuators beyond traditional metal substrates and piezoelectric films to include the optimization of fibers and polarization in laminated piezocomposite multi-entry actuators (LAPAs). Structural characteristics of cantilever piezoelectric harvesters strongly shape their mechanical behavior, especially bending stiffness, deflection, natural frequency, and fatigue response. The evidence points to a beam-based harvester where vibration is concentrated along the length of the cantilever beam, and the design is optimized by changing geometry and substrate shape [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that cantilever beams are fixed at one end and free to vibrate at the other, which is central to understanding how boundary conditions affect mechanical strain and resonance [N2-F2].

### Geometry, bending stiffness, deflection, and thickness-width tradeoffs
Length, width, and thickness are the key geometric variables that affect bending stiffness and deflection. The search evidence explicitly notes that studies investigate length-to-thickness ratio, length-to-width ratio, and substrate effects [N1-R3]. In a practical design study, a trapezoidal hollow structure was used to reduce resonant frequency and increase output voltage, showing how altering cross-section geometry changes the mechanical response [N1-F1]. The same study also optimized a hollow cantilever beam and found that the trapezoidal hollow structure reduced resonance frequency by 12.18% and increased output voltage by 34.67% under the same acceleration [N1-F1]. This implies that thickness and cross-sectional shape directly control stiffness and deflection: thicker or more rigid cross-sections increase stiffness and reduce deflection, while thinner or hollowed structures lower stiffness and allow more deflection.

The review evidence further explains that cantilever beams are free to vibrate at one end, allowing mechanical strain to be concentrated along the length [N2-F2]. This concentration of strain is why geometry matters: changing length, width, or thickness alters the beam’s stiffness and how much it bends under load. The evidence also suggests that material thickness and beam cross-section affect stress distribution, because hollowing or modifying the shape can change the load path and bending behavior [N1-F1]. In other words, geometry does not merely determine where the harvester bends; it determines how it bends and how much stress it carries.

### Boundary conditions and cantilever shape affect natural frequency and resonance
Boundary conditions are central to resonance behavior. The review explicitly frames the cantilever beam as fixed at one end and free at the other, which directly defines the natural frequency and resonance properties [N2-F2]. The optimization study shows how structural changes such as trapezoidal hollowing can tune resonance frequency downward, reducing it by 12.18% in one case [N1-F1]. Another search result on adjusting the resonant frequency of a piezoelectric harvester indicates that methods for changing the resonance are part of cantilever construction [N2-R1]. This suggests that the cantilever shape, end conditions, and internal geometry can shift the resonance frequency.

The same optimization study also indicates that the harvester can be tuned to operate at lower frequencies by changing the beam shape, while still increasing output voltage [N1-F1]. That is important because resonance frequency determines where the harvester is most efficient: the output peak occurs near the resonant frequency, and mismatch with the ambient vibration frequency reduces energy capture. So structural changes that tune the natural frequency are not only mechanical adjustments; they are resonance tuning mechanisms [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### Material thickness and beam cross-section affect stress distribution and fatigue behavior
Material thickness and cross-section also influence stress distribution and fatigue. The optimization study notes that the trapezoidal hollow structure not only lowered resonance frequency but also changed the stress distribution and output performance [N1-F1]. This indicates that cross-sectional geometry affects how load is distributed across the beam. Thicker or more solid cross-sections can support higher stress concentrations, while hollow or truncated shapes can redistribute stress and reduce peak stress in some regions [N1-F1]. The fatigue study cited in the search evidence further confirms that cantilever piezoelectric harvesters experience long-term fatigue behavior under base excitation, showing that repeated mechanical loading affects durability [N2-R2]. Thus, geometry and cross-section are not just about resonance and deflection; they also govern fatigue resistance.

### Bottom line
The structural characteristics of a cantilever piezoelectric harvester are tightly linked to its mechanical behavior. Geometry such as length, width, and thickness changes bending stiffness and deflection [N1-R3][N1-F1]. Boundary conditions and cantilever shape determine natural frequency and resonance [N2-F2][N1-F1]. Material thickness and beam cross-section affect stress distribution and fatigue behavior [N1-F1][N2-R2]. These effects are interdependent: changing one dimension alters the others, and optimization studies show that the best mechanical performance is achieved by balancing stiffness, resonance, and stress distribution [N1-F1].

Structural characteristics affect energy output through their influence on generated voltage and current, as well as through load resistance and vibration conditions. The evidence supports three main mechanisms: geometric and material choices determine the electrical response of the harvester, load resistance controls power transfer and maximum output, and vibration amplitude and frequency content determine how efficiently energy is harvested [N1][N3][N4][N6].

### Harvester dimensions and material choice influence generated voltage and current
The evidence shows that structural design directly affects the electrical response. The optimization study found that a trapezoidal hollow structure reduced resonance frequency by 12.18% and increased output voltage by 34.67% under the same acceleration [N1-F1]. It also noted that the PEH with a trapezoidal hole obtained a power density of 7.24 mW/cm³ [N1-F1]. This demonstrates that structural dimensions and cross-sectional shape can raise voltage output. The search evidence also notes that a hollow rectangular cantilever beam can reduce resonance frequency and increase output voltage [N1-F1], and that hollowing and other structural changes are used to improve harvester performance [N1-R4].

Material choice also matters. The review notes that piezoelectric ceramics such as PZT, PVDF, and other materials are important because they convert mechanical stress into electrical signals [N2-F2]. The material comparison evidence indicates that PZT, AlN, and PVDF differ in performance, with PVDF showing comparatively lower power output and efficiency in one comparison, while AlN demonstrated moderate performance [N4-R1]. Another comparison suggests that PZT has low energy conversion efficiency and is fragile compared to PVDF, making it less suitable for alternating-load applications [N4-R5]. This means that the material selected can change the voltage, current, and overall output capability of the harvester.

### Load resistance and electrical coupling affect power transfer and maximum output
Load resistance is a major determinant of power transfer. The evidence on electrical coupling says that piezoelectric harvesters are usually connected to a load resistor matching the internal capacitance, and that impedance matching is used to maximize harvested power [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The same search result also states that impedance matching networks can be designed to maximize harvested power and improve power efficiency [N6-R5]. This shows that load resistance is not just a passive circuit parameter; it is part of the electrical coupling mechanism.

The review evidence explains that the output power and voltage depend on the load resistance, with the power output curve shaped by the load and the maximum power point determined by the impedance match [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence also indicates that when the circuit works as a negative resistance, current flows into the piezoelectric element, providing an external excitation to the system [N3-R1]. This implies that the electrical coupling is bidirectional: the mechanical motion drives charge generation, and the electrical load determines how much of that charge is converted into usable power.

### Vibration amplitude and frequency content affect energy harvesting efficiency
Vibration amplitude and frequency content matter because the harvester’s output depends on how much motion it receives. The review explains that vibration energy harvesting captures ambient mechanical energy from sources such as acoustics, water flow, wind, human movement, and infrastructure vibrations, and that the harvester converts this into electricity [N2-F2]. The optimization study shows that the same harvester can be tuned to lower frequencies and still produce useful output [N1-F1], suggesting that frequency content is important. However, the evidence also implies that the harvester’s efficiency depends on matching the ambient vibration frequency to the harvester’s resonance frequency.

The search result on adjusting the resonant frequency explicitly says that methods for changing the resonant frequency are part of cantilever construction [N2-R1], and the review notes that the harvester is most effective when the mechanical energy from the source is matched to the device’s operating frequency [N2-F2]. The evidence on electrical response further connects the output to load resistance and power transfer [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Taken together, these sources indicate that higher vibration amplitude increases the mechanical motion available for conversion, while a frequency content that matches the harvester’s resonance frequency maximizes efficiency [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### Bottom line
Structural characteristics affect energy output by changing voltage and current generation, load resistance affects power transfer and maximum output, and vibration amplitude and frequency content determine how efficiently energy is harvested [N1][N3][N4][N6]. Geometry and material choice influence the electrical response, load resistance determines the coupling and maximum power point, and frequency content determines whether the harvester can efficiently capture ambient energy [N2-F2][N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R5].

Mechanical-electrical coupling and resonance matching are central to how a cantilever piezoelectric harvester delivers power. The evidence shows that resonance frequency matching and impedance matching affect power transfer, that mechanical strain is converted into electrical charge and voltage, and that load resistance shapes the power output curve and the maximum power point [N2][N3][N6].

### Resonance frequency matching and impedance matching affect power transfer
Resonance frequency matching is a key mechanism. The review says that vibration-based piezoelectric harvesters consist of a vibrating structure such as a cantilever beam, and that the harvester is most efficient when the ambient vibration frequency matches the device’s operating frequency [N2-F2]. The optimization study also shows that structural changes such as trapezoidal hollowing can tune resonance frequency downward [N1-F1]. This means that if the ambient vibration frequency is close to the harvester’s natural frequency, the mechanical motion is maximized, and the harvester can produce more electrical energy.

Impedance matching is equally important. The evidence states that piezoelectric energy harvesters are usually connected to a load resistor matching the internal capacitance, and that impedance matching networks can be designed to maximize harvested power and improve power efficiency [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The same search result also mentions that a broadband harvester with a coupling resonance frequency tuning mechanism uses variable EEC [N6-R2]. This suggests that both mechanical resonance and electrical impedance need to be matched for optimal power transfer.

### Mechanical strain conversion relates to electrical charge and voltage
The mechanical-to-electrical conversion is the core of the harvester. The review explains that piezoelectric materials convert mechanical stress into an electrical signal, such as polarization, electric displacement, or an electric field [N2-F2]. It also describes the direct piezoelectric effect, where stress produces electric displacement, and the indirect effect, where an electric field produces mechanical response [N2-F2]. This shows that mechanical strain is not only the input but also the driver of charge and voltage generation.

The evidence on electrical response further links the harvester’s output to load resistance. It states that when the circuit works as a negative resistance, current flows into the piezoelectric element, providing an external excitation to the system [N3-R1]. This implies that the harvester generates charge and voltage from mechanical motion, and that the electrical load can modify how that charge is extracted and converted into usable power [N3-R1][N3-R2].

### Load resistance shapes the power output curve and maximum power point
Load resistance determines the shape of the power output curve and the location of the maximum power point. The evidence on electrical response says that output power and voltage depend on load resistance, and that the power output curve is shaped by the load [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The impedance-matching evidence also says that matching the load to the internal capacitance maximizes harvested power [N6-R1], while impedance-matching networks can improve power efficiency [N6-R5]. This means that the power output curve is not flat; it peaks at a particular load resistance, and mismatching the load reduces the maximum output.

The evidence also indicates that the harvester’s output is maximized when the load and the system are impedance-matched. This is important because, in practice, the optimal load resistance is not the same as the one that maximizes voltage or current. Instead, it is the one that best matches the system’s internal impedance and delivers the highest power [N6-R1][N6-R5].

### Bottom line
Mechanical-electrical coupling and resonance matching are essential for power delivery. Resonance frequency matching ensures the harvester is excited near its natural frequency, while impedance matching ensures the electrical load is optimized for power transfer [N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Mechanical strain is converted into electrical charge and voltage through the piezoelectric effect [N2-F2], and load resistance shapes the power output curve and determines the maximum power point [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Together, these effects explain why the harvester’s output is not only a function of the mechanical input but also of the electrical load and resonance conditions.

The design of a cantilever piezoelectric harvester involves important tradeoffs between high stiffness, high output, and low stress fatigue, as well as between thickness and width in resonance tuning and power density. The evidence shows that optimization is driven by geometry, material, and resonance matching, and that practical design is constrained by manufacturability, load impedance, and mechanical durability [N5-F3][N2-F2][N8].

### Tradeoffs between high stiffness, high output, and low stress fatigue
High stiffness is desirable because it increases the natural frequency and improves the harvester’s ability to respond to higher-frequency vibrations [N2-F2][N8]. However, stiffness also increases stress concentration, which can raise fatigue risk under repeated loading [N2-R2][N7]. The fatigue study cited in the evidence explicitly notes long-term fatigue behavior of a cantilever piezoelectric energy harvester under base excitation [N2-R2], showing that high stress can degrade long-term durability.

This creates a central tradeoff: making the structure stiffer can improve resonance and output, but may also increase peak stress and fatigue failure risk. The optimization evidence supports this by showing that structural changes such as hollowing or trapezoidal shaping can tune resonance frequency and increase output without simply relying on conventional geometry [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The topology-optimization paper further explains that the performance of the harvester is limited by the amount of mechanical energy harvested from vibrations and that advanced optimization techniques are used to improve performance by considering geometry, material properties, and electrical load impedance [N5-F3]. This means the optimal design is not just about maximizing stiffness or output in isolation; it is about balancing those goals against fatigue and mechanical robustness.

### How thickness and width affect resonance tuning and power density
Thickness and width are central to resonance tuning and power density. The evidence notes that studies investigate length-to-thickness ratio and length-to-width ratio, and that hollowing or modifying the cross-section changes the mechanical response [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The optimization study shows that a trapezoidal hollow structure reduced resonance frequency by 12.18% and increased output voltage by 34.67% under the same acceleration [N1-F1]. This illustrates how thickness and cross-sectional shape can tune the resonance frequency downward while also increasing output.

Width also matters because it affects the beam’s moment of inertia and bending stiffness. The review evidence explains that cantilever beams are fixed at one end and free at the other, and that the natural frequency and resonance behavior depend on geometry [N2-F2]. The optimization paper further says that the geometry and material properties of the piezoelectric element, the resonant frequency of the device, and the electrical load impedance all need to be considered in optimization [N5-F3]. In practice, this means that increasing width may lower stiffness and lower resonance frequency, while changing thickness can adjust the stress distribution and output performance [N1-F1][N7].

The evidence also connects these geometric choices to power density. The optimized trapezoidal hollow structure achieved a power density of 7.24 mW/cm³ [N1-F1], and the search result on optimizing thickness distribution says the study presents an analytical and experimental approach to enhance cantilever-based piezoelectric energy harvesters [N2-R3]. This shows that thickness and width are not only tuning parameters but also contributors to the overall energy density of the harvester.

### Practical limits and optimization criteria for cantilever design
The practical limits of cantilever design are clear: the harvester must be manufacturable, durable, and efficient enough to meet application requirements. The topology-optimization paper explicitly states that the design requires consideration of manufacturability and that advanced optimization techniques are used to improve performance [N5-F3]. It also mentions that early optimization studies focused on periodic piezocomposites, topology optimization, and multi-domain design, including piezoelectric material, electrode, and substrate domains [N5-F3]. This suggests that the design space is constrained by both physical manufacturability and the need to optimize multiple interacting domains.

The optimization criteria include:
- matching the device’s resonant frequency to the ambient vibration frequency [N2-F2],
- maximizing the electromechanical coupling and piezoelectric effect [N5-F3],
- reducing stress concentrations and fatigue risk [N2-R2],
- optimizing load impedance for maximum power transfer [N6-R1][N6-R5],
- and improving output voltage and power density through geometry and material choice [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5].

In practice, these criteria are often conflicting. For example, a thicker, stiffer beam may increase resonance frequency and reduce fatigue risk, but may also lower the deflection and output voltage [N1-F1][N7]. Conversely, a thinner or hollowed beam may increase deflection and output, but may also increase stress and fatigue risk [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The evidence therefore supports a systematic optimization approach rather than an ad hoc adjustment of one dimension at a time.

### Bottom line
The main design tradeoffs are between high stiffness, high output, and low stress fatigue [N2-R2][N7], while thickness and width affect resonance tuning and power density [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Practical limits and optimization criteria include manufacturability, mechanical durability, impedance matching, and multi-domain coupling [N5-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5]. The optimal cantilever design is therefore a balance of geometry, material, resonance, and electrical load, with topology optimization and multi-objective analysis used to find the best compromise [N5-F3][N2-F2][N8].

## How do the structural characteristics of a cantilever piezoelectric energy harvester affect its mechanical behavior and energy output?

A cantilever piezoelectric energy harvester is fundamentally a mechanical-electrical system: its structural characteristics determine how it bends, vibrates, and responds to external motion, and those same characteristics also shape the amount of electrical energy it can generate. The evidence shows that structural changes such as length, width, thickness, and cross-sectional shape alter bending stiffness, deflection, natural frequency, and fatigue behavior, while material choice and load resistance determine voltage, current, power output, and efficiency [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R5][N6-R1].

### 1) Structural characteristics influence mechanical behavior

The mechanical behavior of a cantilever piezoelectric harvester is dominated by geometry. A cantilever beam is fixed at one end and free to vibrate at the other, which means that any change in length, width, or thickness alters the beam’s stiffness and deflection [N2-F2][N1-R3]. The evidence also notes that hollow or trapezoidal shapes can reduce resonance frequency and increase output voltage, showing that structural cross-sections are not just passive parts of the device but active tuning elements [N1-F1]. In other words, making the beam thicker or more rigid increases stiffness and reduces deflection, while making it thinner or hollowed lowers stiffness and increases bending [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Boundary conditions and cantilever shape are equally important for natural frequency and resonance. Because the beam is fixed at one end, its natural frequency depends on geometry, and structural optimization can shift the resonance frequency to match the ambient vibration environment [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that cantilever shape can be adjusted to tune the first eigen frequency, and that optimization studies use thickness distribution and topology optimization to improve performance [N2-R3][N5-F3]. This is a key point: resonance is not a fixed property of the material alone; it is a function of the structural design.

Material thickness and beam cross-section also affect stress distribution and fatigue behavior. The evidence shows that hollowing or changing the cross-section changes stress distribution, and that long-term fatigue behavior is observed under base excitation [N1-F1][N2-R2]. This means that even when a harvester is designed for higher output, it must be engineered to avoid excessive stress concentrations that could accelerate fatigue failure. The tradeoff is clear: a stiffer, thinner beam may bend more and generate more strain, but it may also carry higher stress and degrade faster over time [N2-R2][N7].

### 2) Structural characteristics affect energy output

Structural characteristics also strongly influence energy output because they affect the electrical response of the harvester. The evidence shows that changes in dimensions and material choice influence generated voltage and current [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5].
